facts.text: The sooty oystercatcher is an all-black wading bird with a red eye, eye ring and bill, and pink legs.
facts.quote: All of its feathers are black. It has a red eye, eye ring and bill, and pink legs.

facts.text: At up to 980 g, it is the heaviest of all oystercatchers, with females larger and heavier than males.
facts.quote: The heaviest of all oystercatchers, the sooty oystercatcher weighs up to 980 g (2.16 lb), averaging around 819 g (1.806 lb), with females larger and heavier in both subspecies.

facts.text: Males have shorter, thicker bills while females have longer, thinner bills—the biggest such difference of any oystercatcher species.
facts.quote: Males have shorter, thicker bills and females have longer, thinner bills. The 19% average difference in length is the most marked of any oystercatcher species.

facts.text: Young birds start with grey-brown legs and brown eyes, gaining their red bill, eyes and legs by their second year.
facts.quote: Immature birds have grey-brown legs, a bill tipped with brown, a browner cast to their plumage, and brown eyes. The bill, eyes and legs become red by the second year.

facts.text: It almost always feeds in the intertidal zone during the two hours either side of low tide.
facts.quote: The sooty oystercatcher almost always forages in the intertidal zone, for the two hours either side of low tide.

facts.text: It lays a clutch of two to three eggs in a rock crevice, hollow, or flat on the ground, often where parents can keep watch.
facts.quote: A clutch of two to three eggs is laid in a crevice in rocks or small hollow or flat on the ground, often on an island or high place where parent birds can keep watch.

facts.text: Its eggs are tapered ovals, buff to beige with dark brown and lavender dots and splotches.
facts.quote: Tapered oval in shape, the eggs are buff to beige with dark brown and lavender dots and splotches and measure 63 mm (2.5 in) long by 42 mm (1.7 in) wide.

facts.text: There are an estimated 11,500 sooty oystercatchers, and the species is listed as Endangered in New South Wales and Rare in South Australia and Queensland.
facts.quote: There are an estimated 11,500 individuals, 4000 of the nominate race and 7500 of the northern race. It is common around the Tasmanian coastline and Bass Strait islands. However it is declared Rare in South Australia and Queensland, Near Threatened in Victoria and Endangered in New South Wales.
